claims.explanation: For x=2 and y=4, the required upper bound is y \leq x^3 = 2^3 = 8, so the condition should be 4 \leq 4 \leq 8. The written expression uses 4^3 instead of 2^3, so it checks the wrong upper bound.

claims.quoted_text: Note that \( x_1^2 \leq x_n \leq x_1^3 \) for all \( n \).
claims.explanation: This is false. Since \(1/2^n \to 0\), \((x_2/x_1)^{1/2^n} \to 1\), so \(x_n \to x_1\), not into \([x_1^2,x_1^3]\). Because \(x_1>1\), we have \(x_1<x_1^2\), so for all sufficiently large \(n\), \(x_n<x_1^2\).
The sequence defined in the previous step tends to \(x_1\), not \(x_2\), because the exponent \(1/2^n\) tends to \(0\).

claims.quoted_text: by the squeeze theorem, \( f(x_n) \to f(x_2) \).
claims.explanation: The squeeze theorem does not apply here: \(f\) is not assumed continuous, and the bounds are the fixed constants \((f(x_1))^2\) and \((f(x_1))^3\), which do not force convergence to \(f(x_2)\).

claims.quoted_text: since \( f(x_1) < f(x_2) \) and \( f(x_n) \) is bounded between two constants, this implies that \( f \) must be continuous
claims.explanation: Boundedness of the sequence \(f(x_n)\) between two constants does not imply continuity of \(f\), nor does it imply \(f(x_n)\to f(x_2)\). No continuity of \(f\) has been established.

claims.quoted_text: \( c^2 \leq c \leq c^3, \) which is true for any \( c \in (1, \infty) \).
claims.explanation: For every \(c>1\), \(c^2>c\), so \(c^2 \leq c\) is false. Thus constant functions with values in \((1,\infty)\) do not satisfy the condition; for example, \(f(x)=x\) is a valid nonconstant solution.
